subtopic: PRIZE COURTS AND PRIZE LAW-EXCHEQUER COURT JURISDICTION

speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 10, to provide for a prize court and prize law in Canada.
He said: The purpose of the bill is to put in statutory form and perhaps make clearer and more definite what is the common law practice in respect to prize courts and prize law jnd to replace the order in council which has oeen in force under the War Measures Act in that regard. I am informed that during the first war the exchequer court as a colonial court of admiralty had jurisdiction as a prize court, and that expired when the old admiralty court act was repealed in 1934. During this war an order in council to give it this jurisdiction was passed under the War Measures Act. It is felt that the jurisdiction of the court should be prolonged beyond the time when the order in council under the War Measures Act will be in force, and this bill is to set out what is the prize law in Canada and to make the exchequer court the court to administer that law.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time. CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF CAPITAL REVISION ACT, 1937- SECURITIES TRUST

speechtext:
Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 11, to amend the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act, 1937.
iMr. Usley.]
He said:	This is a routine and simple amendment of the Canadian Railways Capital Revision Act, 1937. Section 12 of that act provides for the appointment of trustees, and it is therein stated that three of the trustees shall be deputy ministers and two others shall be officers of the Canadian National Railways. By virtue of a reorganization in the directorate one of these positions in the Canadian National Railways, that of vice-president of finance, has been abolished. It is therefore sought by this amendment to set up by way of resolution of the board of directors the two officers who shall be trustees representing that body. There is also a technical amendment which has to do with the three deputy ministers.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

2.	Although all 1943 crop wheat has been disposed of by the board to shippers and mills, the mills have not yet completed their reports to the board as to whether the wheat was used for domestic, mutual aid or commercial flour sales.
Without this information the board cannot determine the amounts per bushel payable on the 1943 crop participation certificates.
Moreover, final payments in respect of the 1940, 1941 and 1942 crops are still being made, and it is estimated that from 65 to 75 thousand cheques have still to be issued covering producer's certificates which have been lost. These operations are all in addition to the current work of the board, which is extremely heavy, and it does not appear that the necessary equipment will be available for the purpose of making this payment until the other payments referred to have been released.

I have considered the advisability of taking further criminal proceedings against Adrien Arcand, who in May, 1940, was charged, by way of indictment, under sections 39 and 39A of the defence of Canada regulations with having spread and published reports and statements intended or likely to cause disaffection or to be prejudicial to the safety of the state or the efficient prosecution of the war. Before the preliminary inquiry was completed and the accused could be committed for trial, the judge directed that the situation disclosed by the evidence should be brought to the attention of the attorney general of Quebec. The latter in turn communicated with the Minister of Justice, who, 'with a view to preventing Arcand from acting in a manner prejudicial to the public safety or the safety of the state, directed that he should be detained, and he was so detained until July, 1945.
It may now be stated that Arcand was the recognized leader of an organization known as the national unity party, declared by the defence of Canada regulations to be illegal. The national unity party had objects and ideals very similar to those of the fascist and nazi parties, and there is evidence of some connecting link between members of those parties and Arcand.
Whether or not the national unity party had any real numerical strength or potential possibilities, the prompt action taken by the Minister of Justice effectively quelled the movement, and the purpose of Arcand and the misguided people whom he sought to influence wholly failed. There is no evidence that his activities or those of the party in fact did any injury or in the slightest degree prejudiced the successful prosecution of the war. My information is that since his release from internment Arcand has not been engaged in any political activity and no complaints have been received with reference to his conduct.
To the question whether further criminal proceedings should be taken against Arcand, the following observations of a legal nature would seem to be relevant:
First, responsibility for the prosecution of indictable offences rests with the provincial attorney general, and, while it would be open to federal authorities to proceed with the charges under the defence of Canada regulations with the object of having Arcand committed for trial, I would not advise this course without first consulting the attorney general of the province, since he must assume responsibility for the trial if the accused is committed.
Secondly, defence of Canada regulations 39 and 39A have been revoked, and, while such revocation does not relieve from liability a person who committed an offence prior to revocation, nevertheless in the case of such a stale offence as this the fact of revocation might be expected to affect the course of the trial.
Thirdly, the maximum sentence which could be imposed for the offences charged is five years' imprisonment. Arcand has already been subjected to confinement for a period in excess of five years.
Fourthly, a proposal to prosecute for a seditious offence under the criminal code would be subject to the same considerations as apply in the case of the charges under the defence of Canada regulations, namely, that the provincial attorney general would be responsible since the proceedings would be by way of indictment, and

that the offence is stale, and that the accused has already suffered a lengthy period of confinement.
Fifthly, Arcand could not be tried for treason for the reason that any such offence has long since been prescribed by statute. In this connection it should be remarked that the Treachery Act of Canada was only assented to on the 7th of August, 1940, after Arcand was interned, and so would not apply to Arcand's activities prior to internment.
Having regard to the foregoing, I would not advise that further criminal proceedings be undertaken by federal authorities, and in this respect I concur in the view recently expressed by Mr. Gerald Fauteux, K.C., who acted as crown prosecutor at the time the charge was laid against Arcand.
F. P. Vareoe,
Deputy Minister of Justice.

Re: Adrien Arcand, Jos. C. Farr et al -Further prosecutions.
Dear Mr. Vareoe,
I have examined the brief submitted for opinion, in relation with the above matter.
This brief, I understand, after a recent interview with Inspector C. W. Harvison of the R.C.M. Police is definitely a general outline ot the case, and cannot be taken as definite and exhaustive as far as evidence is concerned.
Furthermore, I had a conference yesterday, in Ottawa, with Mr. Robert Forsyth, K.C., of your department, with whom I discussed the matter, and who, I may say, agrees with the views which I now beg to express as follows:
1.	The matter during the war:
In the spring of 1940, and as the result of the execution of a number of search warrants, truckloads of documents were seized in various places and in various provinces in Canada.
At that time, more than sufficient evidence was gathered to justify a prosecution under sections 39 and 39A of the defence of Canada regulations. And as a matter of fact, on the 29th of May, 1940, a number of warrants were issued for the arrest of the leaders of the so-called "national social Christian party" and "national unity party of Canada".
According to their own publications, their programme, I quote:
"in its main lines, and even in many details, is identical to the programme of the principal corporatist organizations of other countries:
"Fascists of Italy,
Nazis of Germany,
Cuzists of Rumania,
Francists of France,
Fascists of Great Britain,
Guardists of Australia,

Questions
Nara-ists of Poland,
Nationalists of Switzerland,
Gadja-ists of Yugoslavia,
Rexists of Belgium,
Fascists of Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Bulgaria, the Netherlands, Portugal, etc." The procedures before the court were by way of indictment. In the course of the preliminary inquiry, the presiding judge, after the filing of a number of exhibits, interrupted the procedure, called the attorneys for the prosecution and the defence, for a short conference in his chamber, and immediately after resuming the procedures in court, declared that there was prima facie evidence of a conspiracy against the safety of the state, and suggested that the matter be immediately referred to the attorney general of the province; the inquiry was then adjourned to the following week. This action of the court brought no protests from the defence counsels, (sic)
Accordingly, the matter was immediately referred to the attorney general who, in turn, advised the then Minister of Justice of same and of the extension of the alleged conspiracy beyond the limits of the province of Quebec. An order for internment under section 21 of the D.O.C.R. followed.
The preliminary inquiry was then adjourned sine die.
Later, the question of prosecution for offences under the criminal code of Canada was considered. It was thought that any trial under circumstances then prevailing, would have possibly led to certain agitation and perhaps, and to an unmeasurable extent, defeated the very purpose which the defence of Canada regulations were meant to achieve.
The national emergency prevailing at that time could hardly be met otherwise than by emergency steps which, as stated, were immediately taken.
2.	The matter since the cessation of hostilities:
I have been asked to express an opinion on the actual possibility of prosecutions.
For that purpose, I have considered the Treachery Act and the criminal code of Canada.
(a)	With regard to the Treachery Act:
To supplement for the inadequacy of legis-ation on treason, Canada, like England, has adopted at the beginning of this war, the Treachery Act, 4 George VI, chapter 43. This act was assented to on the 7th of August, 1940, consequently after the internment of Arcand and others. The statute having no retroactive effect, cannot therefore have any application in the matter.
(b)	The Criminal Code of Canada:
1.	Treason and treasonable offences:
I cannot say that the activities of the above group could not reveal evidence of treason or treasonable offences. To express a final and definite opinion, as to a conviction without *doubt, would necessitate a more complete and minute examination of the mass of documents :seized.
The provisions of our code on treason and treasonable offences have their source in the English statute known as the Treason Act assented to in the year 1351, and are far from *suiting modern conditions.
Their enforcement is not, consequently, with

out difficulty.
For practical purposes, however, our Canadian law as well as the English law provide for a limitation of action, and in both countries, it has ahvays been and still is impossible to prosecute after three years.
Under such circumstances, prosecution for treason or treasonable offences cannot be entered.
2.	Drilling:
Drilling was also in the programme of these organizations, and for that reason, provisions of section 99 were examined.
The operation of that section depends upon the existence of an order in council prohibiting training or drilling to the use of arms or for the purpose of practising military exercises, movements or evolutions. I am not aware of the existence of an order in council covering the case.
Be it as it may, these provisions are also subject to a limitation, under section 1140, paragraph "b", subparagraphs "i" and "ii".
In such eases, prosecution may be commenced within six months after the commission of the offence.
S.	133-
3.	Seditious offences: S. 134-
I have also given consideration to the question of sedition. Of that, there is evidence. And in such matters, there is no limitation of action.
To decide whether it is in the best interest of Canada and particularly of justice to the accused as well, you may like to consider the exculpatory clause of section 133A-which I do not believe has, in fact, any application in the matter, but is, in law, nevertheless opened to the accused for their defence at trial-and also the fact that the maximum penalty for the offence is two years imprisonment, while the leaders of the movement have actually been deprived of their liberty for a period of five years, more or less.
Our legislation being inspired by the same principles of justice animating the English legislation, you may also consider that the leaders of a like movement in Great Britain, particularly Sir Oswald Mosley, have not been prosecuted after suffering internment.
Our penal laws operate by punishment, the purpose of -which is double, to wit: punishment to individuals and deterrent for other people.
In view of the length of internment which is more than twice the authorized maximum sentence for sedition, I doubt what more could be achieved in prosecuting for sedition.
And the judgment given by the civilized nations on the ideologies professed by these groups is and shall ever be far more impressive than a judgment of one of our local courts of Quebec or Ontario against a limited number of individuals Treasonably attracted by and promoting these now universally condemned ideologies and purposes.
It is again a timely question whether the publicity attached to trials by the will of the legislator, would not, in this case, be used to serve a purpose much beyond its true object.
Personally, and if I may be permitted to express an opinion as to the advisability of proceeding for sedition, I honestly believe that
Questions

the national interest and the Canadian justice would equally be served adequately by following the policy adopted in the very country from which flows our legislation in similar matters. Yours very truly,

His Excellency
The Governor General in Council:
Whereas the Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, the Prime Minister, reports that by order in council P.C. 134 of January 26, 1924, authority is given for displaying the Red Ensign with the shield of the coat of arms of Canada in the fly (commonly known as "the Canadian Red Ensign") on suitable occasions from all buildings owned or occupied by the Canadian government and situated without Canada;
That the Canadian Red Ensign was employed by Canadian forces during the present w-ar; and
That, until such time as action is taken by parliament for the formal adoption of a national flag, it is desirable to authorize the flying of the Canadian Red Ensign on federal government buildings within as well as without Canada, and to remove any doubt as to the propriety of flying the Canadian Red Ensign wherever place or occasion may make it desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag;
Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, is pleased to order and doth hereby order that the Red Ensign with the shield of the coat of arms of Canada in the fly (hereinafter referred to as "the Canadian Red Ensign") may be flown from buildings owned or occupied by the federal government within and without Canada;
His Excellency in Council, on the same recommendation, is further pleased to declare and doth hereby declare that it shall be appropriate to fly the Canadian Red Ensign within and
without Canada wherever place or occasion may make it desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag.
Nothing herein shall be deemed to alter in any way the provisions now in force with respect to the flying of the Blue Ensign with the shield of the coat of arms of Canada in the fly on Canadian naval vessels and other government vessels, nor with respect to the flying of the Canadian Red Ensign on Canadian merchant vessels.
A. D. P. Heeney,

Function:	The object of the Khaki

The primary purpose of these facilities is to assist the student in effecting the process of readjustment involved in entering upon, or

resuming university studies or vocational pursuits in Canada after repatriation. Without prejudice to this primary object, and in appropriate cases where the progress made in a particular subject warrants, the secondary purpose is to provide, on a voluntary basis, an opportunity for students to write examinations leading to a credit in such subject at a recognized Canadian university.
It is organized in three branches: (1) The Junior college; (2) University Extension; (3) Vocational Extension.
Re (1)-The Junior college provides opportunity for students to take 1st and 2nd year work in Arts and Science, according to courses offered for extramural study by Canadian universities.
Candidates are recommended by commanding officers to the rehabilitation training selection board of their division, or equivalent formation. The function of the board is to pass upon the candidate's eligibility and qualifications and make recommendation to the authorities of the Junior college. Candidates accepted by the registrar of the Junior college are then posted to the college for a term of three months (with provision in certain cases for a second term). During the term, a student may study not more than two subjects. During his attachment to the Junior college, the student receives pay and allowances of his rank. Rations and quarters are provided.
Re (2)-The department provides opportunity for attachment to British universities in any faculty, or students of 3rd and 4th year standing or those qualified for postgraduate study.
Candidates are screened by a committee at Canadian military headquarters with the High Commissioner of Canada as chairman. On being accepted as possessing the qualifications necessary to profit by attachment to a British university, candidates are certified to the principal of the university of their choice, or, if no vacancies remain at that institution, places are secured at some other university offering the studies desired by candidates. All students attached to British universities receive pay and allowances of their rank together with a ration allowance. They must themselves pay for all tuition and all living costs.
Re (3)-The department provides opportunity for attachment to British technical institutes, agricultural schools, industries, of those deemed qualified to profit by such attachment.

MEMORIAL CROSS TO FOSTER MOTHER OF SERVICEMAN KILLED IN ACTION
speechtext: What consideration, if any, has been given to the amending of order in council P.C. 4210 (as amended by P.C. 2135) to make possible the granting of the Memorial Cross to the foster mother of a serviceman who gave his life while a member of the Canadian armed forces?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
maintopic: MEMORIAL CROSS TO FOSTER MOTHER OF SERVICEMAN KILLED IN ACTION
speechtext:
The question of extending the award of the memorial cross to foster mothers and others was carefully reviewed in June, 1944 and is was considered inadvisable to extend the scope of issue for the reasons following:
The governing orders in council (P.C. 4210 of 27 August, 1940 as amended by P.C. 2135 of 28 March, 1943) provide for the issue of the cross "as a memento of personal loss and sacrifice on the part of mothers and widows of Canadian sailors, soldiers, airmen or merchant seamen who have laid down their lives fpr their country during the present war", from which it will be seen that the cross is intended as a recognition of the great sacrifice arising from the closest family ties.
Whereas the sacrifice does not permit of tangible recognition, nevertheless the memorial cross was instituted as a symbol of the personal loss suffered by a mother or widow whose sense of loss is necessarily deeper than that of others, and in order to preserve the underlying sentiment of the award it is felt that it must be restricted in this manner to those bearing the very closest and most clearly determinable ties of relationship.

subsubtopic: QUESTION OF GRANTING CLEAR TITLES TO LAND HELD UNDER CONTRACT ON MARCH 31, 1944
speechtext:
Whereas veterans of great war I who settled on land under the soldier settlement scheme as well as their wives and families, have in many instances suffered severe hardships because of purchase of land, live stock and equipment at inflationary prices, and low prices received for farm products brought about by lack of adequate policy for agriculture;
And whereas we are now embarking on another land scheme for veterans of the present war, under a government policy that does not guarantee cost of production, the success of which scheme may be jeopardized by the apparent failure of the former soldier settlement board scheme;
Therefore be it resolved.-that, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of giving clear titles to all soldier settlers who on March 31, 1944, held land under contract with the soldier settlement board.
He said: I am very glad to have the opportunity of again taking up this question on the first private members' day made available after the close of the war, which I believe is now finished. I want it plainly understood in regard to what I shall have to say on behalf of the soldiers for whom I am speaking that they are not asking for any charity. I also want it plainly understood that I am not a soldier settler, nor am I in any way indebted to the soldier settlement board.
This question, as I have stated before, is one of long standing, and I hope that in the very near future it will be disposed of to the benefit of those interested and to the credit of the Canadian people.
Some people may feel that there is no justice in this matter. Personally I feel quite differently about it, and before I am through I hope to show that several other Canadians feel exactly the same as I do.
I am bringing this matter up at this time, as I have brought it up in past years, because the men who return from this war and who are going to settle on the land under the present Veterans' Land Act will be in a position similar to that of the veterans of the first
Soldier Settlement

great war unless we take care now to see that the old veterans are dealt with as they should have been years ago.
In order to show that these men have some claim, as have the men who are coming back from this war, I am going to read from an address delivered by the late Sir Robert Borden to the Canadian expeditionary force away back in 1917. This may sound old, but in my opinion it forms a basis for the claim that is made by these old soldier settlers. I quote:
You are the men actually facing the enemy day and night. You are suffering greatly from fatigue, overstrained, and lack of rest. The marvel of it is that men could undergo such a strain without breaking; but you have never yet broken, and history will appreciate that in days to come.
You are men about to enter one of the most serious engagements that ever faced the Canadian corps. I cannot, at this moment, give any information as to where this attack will be staged; whether it be successful or not, it is to be borne in mind1 that it will not be an easy success. . . . We feel confident that you will succeed where others failed, for you have neveT yet failed in anything you have set your hand to, as a Canadian corps.
You can go into this action feeling assured of this, and as the head of the government, I give you this assurance; that you need have no fear that the government and the country will fail to show just appreciation of your service to the country and empire in what you are about to do and what you have already done. The government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of the people at home, and it will always be our endeavour to so guide the attitude of public opinion, that the country will support the government to prove to the returned man its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and empire; and that no man, whether he goes back, or whether he remains in r landers, will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken with the men who won and the men who died.
This matter of granting simple justice to the veterans of great war I is not a new one. I have in my hand a copy of a brief which was presented to the members of the Senate and the House of Commons in 1938, after quite a lot of work had been done by a committee at that time. Let me read one paragraph from the introduction:
It is only fair to state at the outset that it is our opinion that the large expenditure of taxpayers' money on these remedial measures and for the settlement scheme has failed utterly to accomplish its purpose, viz.-the ultimate ownership, within a reasonable period of time, of his home in the country for which he fought during the war.
That is from the brief presented by the Soldier Settlers Union, with headquarters at Lloydminster, of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
rMr. Fair.]
I will not dwell on that, but I have a number of figures which I think it is necessary to place on the record in order that the case of the old veterans will be studied by the many new members we have here, and I hope they will give us the backing which the old veterans deserve. I am asking this because many service personnel have returned irom overseas, and there are a number of men elected to this house whose duty it is to see that the men who come back from this war and settle on the land and in other occupations are properly dealt with by the government.
This is not a political matter. The men for whom I am speaking are all Canadians, as are the men who are returning now and who have returned from the recent conflict. The total number of settlers under the old soldier settlement board scheme was 25,017. The total amount advanced by the government of the day for the purchase of land, live stock and equipment was $109,034,331. The rate of interest on that amount was five per cent on current account, seven per cent as soon as the account went into arrears; and I think it will be readily understood that, because of the conditions that obtained at that time, namely, the high prices paid for land, live stock and equipment and the low prices that very soon prevailed for agricultural products, the men went into arrears and as a result were faced with the problem of paying seven per cent interest on their debts.
Here may I say that had the government of the day done its duty it would not have been necessary to pay seven per cent on that money, or five per cent, or even 3i per cent. It would appear however that the golden calf, or the golden bull as some people call it, had to be worshipped instead of the rights of the men who went and fought for Canada, being preserved. I will give the total principal repaid from the inception of the scheme up to March 31, 1944-and I am making that cut-off because, if we let this thing drag on for a little while, we shall find the old saying coming true, that-
Old soldiers never die, never die. never die;
Old soldiers never die; they simply fade away.
That will be realized, I say, and the government will have some more land for sale, perhaps to aliens, and at much less than the amount against it at the present time.
The total amount of principal repaid by everybody under that scheme, that is, the settlers themselves, civilians to whom land was sold after the soldier settler had vacated it, and British families and others, was $50,507,493.20. The total amount of interest was $25,381,060.13, making a total of $75,888,-

Soldier Settlement
553.33. Because of the conditions that existed at that time the government found it necessary to take many methods of reducing the debts of the settlers, in other words of rectifying the unjust contract into which these men had entered. As a result of seven or eight different processes there was a total amount cancelled on account of soldier settler debts of $24,867,637.64 of principal, and interest to the amount of $19,234,239.77, making a total of $44,101,877.41. Up to the end of March, 1944, the cost of administration of the soldier settlement part of the scheme alone amounted to $27,340,763.64. That, I might say, represents an annual expenditure of cost of administration of approximately $1,100,000. The amounts that I have just given total $71,442,641.05.
Then again we have other cancellations that were made necessary because of the civilians, British families and others, who bought this land after the soldier settlers got off. These amounts were as follows: For civilians, principal $2,403,489.46; interest $2,518,264.86; British families, principal $4,485,087.05; interest $3,304,596.49; other families for principal $383,656.07, and interest $294,244.17. These items added together make a total of $7,272,232.58 for principal, and $6,117,105.52 for interest. The grand total $13,389,338.10.
We now add to this the amounts of cancellations of the soldier settlers, which totals $71,442,641.05, and also the general land administrative expenses of $3,376,548.32. Adding all this together gives us a total of $88,208,527.47. This is the amount of cancellations and administrative expenses, and we have up to the end of March collected only $50,507,493.20 in principal and $25,381,060.13 in interest, making a total of $75,888,553.33.
From these figures I think it will be clearly seen that the scheme was a sadly and badly improvised one and impossible right from the start. As I have pointed out on other occasions, the government would have saved money, and the soldier settlers who settled under that scheme would have been saved a whole lot of misery, poverty and punishment, if the government had adopted a scheme of giving them the land without one cent being charged against them.
At the end of March, 1944, the soldier settlers owed a total of $7,715,954.01; the civilian settlers under that scheme owed $6,999,197.40, the British families owed $1,895,612.66, and others $122,333.98, making a total amount outstanding at the end of March, 1944, of $16,733,098.05. The total amount of arrears owed by soldier settlers at that date was
$1,054,269.30; civilian settlers $616235.77; British families and others $205,794.91, making a grand total of arrears as at March 31, 1944, of $1,876,269.98. At that time there were 6,153 soldier settlers still holding contracts with the board, or approximately 25 per cent of the original number of settlers. At the same time we had 5,715 civilian settlers and 1,163 British families and others, making a total of 13,031 settlers still on the land and holding contracts with the board.
I am not making any plea to-day on behalf of the British families and others. What I am principally interested in is the old soldier settler, but I had to bring in these figures to give a complete picture of the financial standing of the soldier settlement board.
The average original debt at the time these men took up the land was $4,358.40. The average balance owing by the settlers still on the land at the end of March, 1944, was $1,254, which represents 29 per cent of their original debt at the time they settled on the land. The number who acquired title during those twenty-five years is 4,130 settlers, or 16 per cent of the 25,017 who originally settled on the land. I think this should make some people sit up and take notice.
I think it should be noted that a number of the old soldier settlers enlisted for service in the war just ended, and in many cases the reason was not patriotism. In fact I know of some who enlisted who could not make a living on the land for their wives and families, and because of the inducements in the form of dependents' allowances and pay for the soldier himself, many of those men enlisted. I may say that they could not make a living on the land, for different reasons. One of the reasons is that we had seventy cent wheat at Fort William until the first of August, 1942. That meant an average of about forty-five cents a 'bushel on the veterans' farm in the prairie provinces. Then we had corresponding prices for other farm produce. After these men enlisted, their wives and families were left home to look after the land. Perhaps the crops were not as good as they should have been, and payments were not coming into the board. The then minister of mines and resources, perhaps prompted or prodded by his director of soldier settlement, decided that something must be done about it, and as a result on March 19, 1941, order in council P.C. 138/1936 was passed by the treasury board on the recommendation of the then minister of mines and resources. The effect of that order in council was to permit the soldier settlement board to deduct up to $20 a month from the money paid the dependents
Soldier Settlement

of these men who had enlisted for the second time, though that money rightfully belonged to the wives and families of those soldiers, for the purpose of making good the payments to the soldier settlement board. In view of the address made to these men in 1917 by the late Sir Robert Borden I wonder if we as a government were keeping faith with the men who went over and fought, particularly when they offered their services and joined up for the second time.
Then on November 19, 1942, another order in council was passed, supposedly for the benefit of these old soldier settlers. You will note that up to this time they had been given some twenty-three or twenty-four years in which to pay for their land, but were not able to do so. During those years they were giving the very best they had; they were in the prime of life. At the end of that time their land was run down to a certain extent, and their implements and live stock had not improved over the years. So in order to make it possible for them to continue to worship the golden calf, order in council P.C. 10472 was passed on November 19, 1942, providing for the setting up of a committee which, if it saw fit, could recommend to the treasury board that the time for payment of the debt on the land could be extended another twenty years. That meant a total of forty-five years for a veteran of the first great war to pay for his farm. The committee also could recommend to treasury board that the debts of various settlers be reduced, and it had also power to recommend that the interest paid by those settlers who enlisted for the second time might be reduced to 3i per cent.
Those things were brought about because of pressure put on the settlers by the officials of the soldier settlement board. If anyone wants to get a picture of the conditions under which many of these settlers are living, it will be found that a large number are living alone, putting up with things which Canada should not allow any of its citizens to put up with, and particularly old soldier settlers. Several attempts have been made to get action; I think we all realize that when we are hard pressed we are liable to do something about it. So in April, 1943, the settlers of the prairie provinces called a meeting at Saskatoon, at which I believe four resolutions were passed, and again in November of 1943 a meeting was held in the same city. Among other things, those attending that gathering decided to circulate a petition during the winter. Those men had no money; they had to start out on their own, but by raising nickels and dimes they were able to obtain enough money to send a delegation to Ottawa a little later on.

As a result of their work 12,500 signatures were obtained to a petition, and on May 23, 1944, a delegation of nine, representing that organization, came to Ottawa and met members of the cabinet.
That meeting was presided over by the then minister of mines and resources, who has since gone to a place of rest; and I may add that with the exception of the chairman all the members of the committee expressed the opinion, either privately or publicly, that this thing should be cleaned up. These men were promised consideration, and we expected they would get it; but of course being promised consideration by members of the cabinet does not always mean that the consideration is going to be in the interests of those asking for it. That consideration was promised in spite of the fact that in the May 1944 issue of The Legionary, the official organ of the Canadian Legion, an article appeared dealing with this very matter. In the pages preceding those containing this article we find advertisements dealing with International Nickel, Canada Post Office, O'Keefe's Brewing Company, Canadian Legion cigarettes, and so on. Then on page 10 we see a picture of the governor general and a little girl under which this caption appears:
Five-year old Carole Louise Hooey, of Toronto, proudly clings to the Distinguished Flying Cross won by her father, the late F/O Gilbert Hooey, who lost his life serving as a pilot overseas.
Then in the lower right hand corner we see a picture of Lieutenant General Sir Richard Turner, V.C., of Quebec City, extending the glad hand of welcome to Major Paul Triquet, whom we had the honour of welcoming here in Ottawa. This is a beautiful setting, interesting and patriotic, for one of the most scurrilous attacks that could be waged against the old soldier settlers by one of our civil servants, who apparently is in good financial circumstances and whose security in old age no doubt is provided for. I am just going to read the opening and closing words. The body of the article deals with figures which are entirely onesided. The article is beaded, "Soldier Settlement" and is written by Gordon Murchison, director, Soldier Settlement and Veterans' Land Act. The first paragraphs of the article read:
Editor, The Legionary-
During the last several months a number of representations have been received by my minister, the Hon. T. A. Crerar, and by myself from and/or on behalf of an organization formed in Saskatoon last summer and known as the soldier settlers association. This association has declared its policy by a resolution, part of which calls for the cancellation of all unpaid balances due or accruing in the agreements between soldier settlers and the director representing

Soldier Settlement
the dominion government. I understand the dominion executive of the Canadian Legion has received similar representations, and so that the situation from the standpoint of the government-
I ask hon. members to note those words-
-and the administration may be placed fairly before the Canadian Legion and the readers of The Legionary, the Hon. Mr. Crerar has authorized me to furnish you with an official statement.
A statement, let me repeat, of arrogance and impudence.
First of all there is lack of evidence that the resolution and representations above referred to reflect the serious views of more than ten per cent of soldier settlers and, knowing the situation as I do, I am sure the great majority of the remaining ninety per cent must feel somewhat humiliated by the publicity being circulated by the few who for reasons best known to themselves and their friends endeavour to paint a dark and gloomy picture. What are the facts?
Before going further I am going to give some of the facts, to disprove some of the information, or misinformation, as you may prefer to call it, contained in this article. Those supporting the request of the old-veterans include over 12,500 signers of a petition; the Alberta legislature; the Saskatchewan legislature; the Alberta farmers union; the Saskatchewan association of rural municipalities; the Saskatchewan wheat pool; the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section; the United Farmers of Alberta and the Alberta branch of the Canadian Legion. In case there should be any mistake about some of the resolutions, I shall read one or two passed by the Canadian Legion at a provincial convention held in Memorial Hall, Edmonton, on June 6 to 9, 1943. This is the first:
Whereas the majority of original soldier settlers, who are still endeavouring to carry on under the soldier settlement scheme have now found it, owing to advanced years and the adverse conditions prevailing in agriculture, particularly the lack of parity prices, increasingly difficult to liquidate their indebtedness to the settlement board,
And whereas the settlers have struggled on through the years of drought conditions and low prices unprecedented in the agricultural history of this country and have now nothing to show for their years of toil and struggle but whatever equity they may have in the land which is liable to foreclosure,
Therefore be it resolved that w-e now petition the government to relieve the soldier settler of any further payments and that they be given the title deed to their land or, failing this, that a parliamentary committee in conjunction with representation from the dominion command of the Canadian Legion, review the whole situation of the soldier settler with a view to alleviating their present financial difficulties.
The second resolution was as follows:
Whereas it has come to our notice that by order in council the soldier settlement board has been permitted to order deductions made from the pay and allowances of dependents of men now serving in the armed forces to be applied against land and taxes,
Therefore we ask that this order in council, be rescinded immediately, and that any sums of money so deducted be refunded.
In addition to the organizations to which I have referred, we also have the executive of the British Columbia branch of the Canadian Legion, and several others which I shall not take time to list. After giving the side of the story pleasing to the director and the government, the director concludes in this manner.
In the face of the above factual information, what is the logic behind the argument that soldier settlers of record to-day should have their contract indebtedness cancelled, which means in effect legislation into ownership? Do the sponsors of the petition believe that this would be the end of the matter? Do they think for a moment that those who have paid for their farms, and all those who are meeting the terms of their agreements in full and on time or are prepaying their agreements, would stand quietly by and make no demand for a refund? I have received direct assurances that such demands would be made.
In reply to the last argument I have asked for the names and copies of the letters which would justify or back up this claim; ajid the answer I got in July, 1944, I believe it was, was to the effect that the representations were made in confidence to the director and members of his organization. To my mind the letters are not there, and cannot be produced. Then, to proceed with the quotation:
Do the petitioners behind this movement consider that they alone have rendered service to the state which outshines the service of tens of thousands of other veterans of the last war who have paddled their own canoes during good times and bad but never asked for or received a dollar of state aid toward the purchase of a home?
These are the questions which give some food for thought and illustrate -why legislation into ownership involves a great deal more than appears at first glance.
Under the heading "No change" we find this:
In conclusion I am authorized to say that the proposal is not deemed to be in the public interest and, consequently, it is not being entertained by the government. Therefore, the best advice I can offer to the soldier settlers concerned is to get into step with those who manifestly prefer securing title to their farms by complying with the terms of their agreements.
Let me point out here that those old soldier settlers are not in receipt of guaranteed government salaries. They have to fight the elements in producing crops, and after they
Soldier Settlement

have done that they have got to fight monopolies on each of the markets on which their produce is sold.
Nothing was done until parliament was prorogued. Then late in August the Minister of Mines and Resources made a radio announcement to the effect that the petitions of the old soldier settlers would not be granted.
In October, 1944, feeling that the Prime Minister did not know the exact situation, I made a special trip to Ottawa, at which time I laid the case before him in his own home in this city. He told me that in the following week the Department of Veterans Affairs would be set up, and that he would turn the matter over to the minister of that department.
I am quite satisfied that the Minister of Veterans Affairs is sympathetically inclined to the granting of titles. If he is not sympathetic, I should like him to tell us now. If he says no, then we shall have some argument at a later time. Apparently he is satisfied that those titles should be granted.
In the next week the department was set up, but nothing has been done up to the present time. As a result of no action being taken, the president and secretary of the settler's organization accompanied me when I visited Ottawa in March of this year, upon which occasion we called upon the Minister of Veterans Affairs and afterwards upon the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Veterans Affairs who apparently had certain objections prepared for him told us that payments were being made, and also that if titles were granted to the old settlers, the new settlers would want free titles also.
I shall deal later with the question of payments; but in connection with the new veterans not wanting to pay up, may I say I would not think the Minister of Veterans Affairs would admit that the new scheme had proved to be a failure, and that the veterans could not pay up; because if they could pay I am quite satisfied that every one, both new and old, would pay. They want to live up to their agreements if at all possible.
After a little while we went on to see the Minister of Finance. While we were received very cordially we did not get very far. He told us that payments were coming in freely, and that he also believed in the sanctity of contract. In connection with payments coming in freely, my comment would be that we have had three good crop years in western Canada, and that prices have been better than they were in other years, both for grain and for live stock. In many instances the families of those old settlers were engaged in war industries, and many of the boys had gone over-
TMr. Fair.]
seas. Well, they were pouring money home to make the old homestead safe for their folks, so that those old people would have a roof over their heads and the boys would have a home to come to when they returned.
Those are some of the reasons. Then, again, dependents' allowances are being used in some cases to make payments. Many of those old settlers and their families went without the necessities of life. One of the delegates who came here in May, 1944 had, shortly before that time, lost his wife. If she had had proper medical attention he would not have suffered that loss.
The fear of eviction will drive many people to do things they would not do otherwise. I think all hon. members can realize the position in which the old settler would find himself if he had no home. Some say, "Oh, well, the soldier settler would not be evicted." Let me contradict that suggestion, because in a return brought down to this house we find that between 1930 and 1942 soldier settlers to the number of 1,006 signed quit-claim deeds. I do not wish anyone to think that they signed those quit-claims voluntarily, because in many cases a good deal of pressure was put upon them, and after signing quit-claim deeds, they got off. And in nearly a thousand cases during the same period, settlers were served with thirty-day notices to get off. That is no worse than the mortgage companies have done -those fellows against whom many of us in this house have railed. Between April 1, 1941, and March 31, 1943, no less than 253 settlers signed quit-claim deeds and 108 settlers were served with thirty-day notices. During the war those men were forced to pay up-or else.
In connection with the sanctity of contracts I want to say that the government made agreements with these men to pay a certain amount for the land. At that time the price of the land was based upon the price of the produce that was being raised on the land. For instance, in many cases wheat was selling at close to $3 a bushel; cows were worth $125 to $150 apiece and horses were worth up to $500 a team and perhaps more. Those are the prices that prevailed at the time those land contracts were made. If the government saw fit to allow those prices to drop down to 20 cents a bushel for wheat, $50 a team for horses and $10 for milch cows, then it was their duty to drop the price of the land in accordance with those prices.
In conclusion I am once more, and I hope I will have plenty of company, asking for clear titles for these men, these old settlers, who held contracts with the soldier settler board at March 31, 1944. In doing that we will be granting nothing more than simple

Soldier Settlement
justice. We will be placing human values before money values. To sum up, 25,017 settlers had an average credit of $4,358.40 under the scheme. At the present time 6,153, or 25 per cent, have an average debt of $1,254. A total of 4,130, or 16 per cent, were able to secure titles in twenty-five years. The rate of interest under the old scheme was five per cent on current debts and seven per cent on arrears, while under the Veterans' Land Act it is 3i per cent or one-half the old rate. Under the present scheme a settler who takes full advantage of the scheme will get a clear grant of $2,320 provided he lives up to the terms of his contract during the first ten years, which is equal to 39 per cent of the total amount of his credit. The average amount owed by the old settlers is only twenty-nine per cent.
Why not give them all a square deal? As I said before, these old fellows were Canadians. I am not speaking of them as being Liberals or Conservatives or of any other political faith. They are Canadians who fought for Canada. The average debt of these old vets is only twenty-nine per cent of original credit extended to them. The shooting war with the enemy is over; let us conclude our war with the old vets, because war it has been for a number of years. The average age of these old settlers is close to sixty years, and to my personal knowledge some of them are over eighty years of age. Yet we are giving these old fellows another term extension of twenty years in which to pay up their debts. Do I see many red faces around here? Can Canada afford nothing better?
The record of payments during the last few years has been obtained at the expense of the health and welfare of the settlers and their families. Coming back to monetary values, we know that during the heat of the war it was costing us more than $16,000,000 a day to send presents to Mussolini, Hitler and Tojo. A total of $7,715,000 will clear off these debts, less than the cost of one-half day of war. If you want to treat it as a direct tax, it amounts to sixty-five cents per capita for the population of Canada. Can we afford it?
I do not feel that I should say very much more about this matter, but there is one thing I want to emphasize. I hope the men who settle on the land under the Veterans' Land Act will not find themselves evicted as many of these old settlers have been. If the land is purchased on the basis of prices being paid for agricultural products to-day, the government should see that credit is made available for the difference between prices that are existing to-day and those that may exist in
the future. If that is not done, we will have a bunch of bankrupt veterans of this war. Let it never be said of us:
We love our nation's heroes dead,
We very much adore 'em;
And since they haven't to be fed,
We build grand tombstones o'er them.
We want our heroes alive; we want them living in the prosperity which this country can very well afford. The welfare of the old vets is inseparably bound up with the future success of those settling under the Veterans' Land Act. Issue those clear titles now and ensure success for the veterans of this war.

subsubtopic: QUESTION OF GRANTING CLEAR TITLES TO LAND HELD UNDER CONTRACT ON MARCH 31, 1944
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first to compliment the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) upon his persistence in keeping this matter before this house. He did so during the life of the last parliament and he is doing so again in this new parliament. As a matter of fact, one of the results of his persistence was that the minister who was dealing with this particular matter in the last parliament was induced to retire to the senate. I hope the present minister, who I know is sympathetic, will not be forced to make a similar decision before this parliament is over.
This matter is not political; it is a case of dealing with the men of the last war. I intend to deal with it from just a little different angle from that of the hon. member for Battle River. He stated in his opening remarks that he was not a soldier settler and therefore was not primarily interested in the matter from a selfish point of view. I am a soldier settler who settled under the act in 1919. For twenty-three years I made payments to the settlement board. I settled in a part of Canada where ther was the greatest concentration of settlers under the act in all the dominion. I have been intimately connected with these men in veterans' and farm organizations for the past twenty-three years, and I know something about the conditions under which they have lived and endeavoured to pay their debts. I want to deal with the matter more from a humanitarian or personal angle.
The hon. member for Battle River gave some figures which I am not going to repeat. He placed many of these figures on the pages of Hansard during the last parliament and has repeated many of them this afternoon. This matter was raised in the committee which dealt with veterans' affairs in 1941 and at that time various objections were raised by the government. One objection was that we were starting a serious conflict which would require all the resources of Canada, both financial and material, and that it was a poor time to drop payments to the dominion government when
Soldier Settlement

the government was entering into financial obligations which would strain its every endeavour. We are now through that period; we have spent millions, if not billions, and that excuse cannot be used.
Another excuse given for not dealing with this matter was that the men who had completed their payments under the act would feel that an injustice was being done and might think that the government should pay back to them some of the money they had paid. As an old settler who has met and talked with many other old settlers, many of whom made a success under the act and met their obligations and many others who failed and took other positions in which they made successes, I believe I can safely say that I do not think there would be one per cent of the old settlers who would object to some alleviation being granted as far as the present debts are concerned. The men who have not been able to meet their obligations and who under the legislation passed recently have had their debts spread over another twenty to twenty-five years have done their best but have met with circumstances over which they had no control which made it impossible for them to meet their obligations. To bear me out in that, I am going to quote extracts from letters which I have received from soldier settlers during the past few years, and I quote them, not to support individual cases, but because they represent a class of case and because the reasons given for failure to meet obligations apply not only to the individual writer but to a large group of soldier settlers.
In the first place, a large number who were settled under the act were settled in the drought area in Saskatchewan, in the Pelliser Triangle, where for years they suffered under drought conditions which made it absolutely impossible for them to meet their obligations under the act. I quote from a letter from one of these men:	The amendment which provided dollar for dollar payments was made, I think in 1937, and there were a large number of the soldier settlers in the south of the province who in that year and in the year following were unable to meet their payments because of drought conditions over which they had no control. This soldier settler writes:
During the drought period a dollar for dollar bonus on arrears was offered. As we had no crops at all we could not take advantage of it. and now when things are a little easier it is discontinued, which is distinctly unfair to the people who need it the most.
Hon. members know that it was 1941 or 1942 before we had a real crop in western Canada and before many of these settlers had a chance

to meet their obligations. But in 1941 the dollar for dollar bonus was discontinued. He
goes on to say:
Secondly, the soldier settlement board paid the taxes w'hich were afterwards cancelled, but are still charged against us with accruing interest, placing us in a worse position than civilians.
As the writer states, the soldier settlement board in 1938 or 1939 took over and paid all the taxes owing and charged1 them against the principal of the loan. A year or so later these taxes were cancelled for civilians but remained a debt so far as the soldier settler was concerned. He goes on to say:
To illustrate this, my original loan was $1,500. I reduced this to $800 before the drought. It now stands at over $1,7DO. These figures may not seem very large, but they are to us.
There is another class of settler, those who were unable to meet their obligations because of sickness in their family or their own sickness. I quote from one of these letters, which shows quite clearly the position in which a large number of these settlers found themselves. The writer says:
Then, seven years ago, came my wife's illness, lasting over three years, with several operations and then her death. This easily added one thousand dollars to my debt and to-day I am paying a housekeeper in wages nearly as much as the payment to the soldier settlement board comes to in a year. Besides my two children, I have my father, nearly ninety years of age. to care for, so I am badly handicapped, and I have fifty per cent disability myself.
This man has a fifty per cent disability. Yet the soldier settlement board, under an order in council passed on March 19, 1941,
states:
The director of soldier settlement has no authority to carry such accounts indefinitely and it is considered desirable to provide for deductions from dependents' allowances to cover local taxes and interest due.
And the board took $10 a month out of this man's pension to meet the payments on bis loan.

subsubtopic: QUESTION OF GRANTING CLEAR TITLES TO LAND HELD UNDER CONTRACT ON MARCH 31, 1944
speechtext:
Yes. There is another class of case. A great many of our settlers under the old act were settled on unsuitable, marginal land, and because of that fact were unable to meet their obligations to the government. I state these things because they show in a great many cases that "hard core" which the department speaks of, was caused by circumstances over which the soldier settler had no control, such as drought, sickness, unsuitable land.
Another factor which operated against the old soldier settler was lack of capital with which to break his land and bring it under

Soldier Settlement
cultivation. The soldier settlement board made a certain allowance for the breaking of the land, but there was so much red tape that many settlers could not take advantage of it. I have letters here which, if I read them to the house, would prove definitely that the red tape which was attached to these loans often made it impossible for the soldier settler to take advantage of them.
Another factor has been the interest rate which was charged on the old loan, six per cent once the payments became overdue, and five per cent on the original loan. This meant that many settlers paid the original loan several times over. Here is a letter which illustrates that point. The writer says:
As you are aware, there have been several adjustments since the original scheme was introduced. The last adjustment was made in my case in 1939, under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. and then my quarter was revalued at $1,800. although I had paid over $3,000 under the original agreement. Since then, although the price of wheat has been very low, I have been able to keep up my payments, but not when due. viz.. October 1. For the last two years it has been impossible, through restricted deliveries and quotas to make payments when due, but the board charge compound interest, which I have refused to pay. It sems incredible that the government should take advantage of this situation to make additional profits, but this is the case. I would point out that since 1939. not including due payment this fall. I have paid the board four payments of each $124.23, some $496, but you will notice I have not reduced the principal yet by $100-some $80 in fact. Surely this would appear to be heavy interest without charging compound interest on top.
That is the position in which many of these old soldier settlers find themselves, and I think it is only simple justice that we in this parliament should take action to relieve them. Under the new land settlement act we have provided much better conditions for the soldiers coming back from this war than were provided under the old act, and in simple justice this parliament should take action to relieve some of the suffering of many of these old soldiers under the old act.
There is another injustice under the old act, and while there are not many cases in which this has happened there are some where the soldier settler under the old act had two quarter-sections of land, one of which he bought through the board and one which he had as a homestead before going overseas. Later, when he came back the board took a mortgage on both pieces of land before they would give him stock and equipment under the act, and in some cases the soldier disposed of one of these quarters to another settler or another individual. Later, this particular individual made application under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement
Act to have his debt reduced and in some cases the board allowed the reduction. Strange to say that reduction was charged back against the old quarter of the soldier settler. That seems to me to be absolutely unjust, because under the old agreement, under the Soldier Settlement Act, the soldier was liable to the board for the full amount of indebtedness; he had disposed of one quarter and later on, perhaps three years after he had disposed of it, that quarter came under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and the debt was reduced, the amount of reduction being charged back to the original quarter of the soldier settler.
I do not know how many cases there were of this kind but there were some. The fact that there is this old core of dissatisfaction under the old act is causing many of the younger soldiers, younger men coming back from this war, to hesitate about again entering into any agreement with the government in regard to land, and I think it would be to the advantage of the government to clear up this matter immediately and to start with a clean slate under a new act. If they do not do so it will simply mean a lot of grief and trouble to them later on, because in areas where you get a few old settlers who have a just complaint, and a group of new men coming in under the new act, invariably the older men will get in contact with the new men and tell their story and dissatisfaction will arise among the newer group. I am sure the new men who settle under the new act, seeing they are getting a better deal than the old soldiers received under the old act, would not use that as a pry to try to get some further consideration from the government as far as meeting their obligations is concerned.
I hope that the new minister will take this matter into serious consideration. As the hon. member for Battle River stated, a delegation came here over a year ago to interview the government. They were certainly given some encouragement by the government to believe their case would be considered after they had gone home, but they found, through the article which the hon. member has just quoted, and from what took place in the veterans' convention in Vancouver, that their case was being passed up as far as the government was concerned. They again came to Ottawa and placed their position before the government. I do not know what the result of the last interview was. I do not know whether they were given encouragement in that last interview, but certainly they have a just case, and I would urge the government to take that case into consideration and do
Soldier Settlement

as suggested in this resolution-cancel the old debt that remains. It is a very small amount in comparison with the expenditures that are made to-day, and I am sure that any action along that line would be appreciated by the old settlers and would be an encouragement to the new men who are returning to settle under the new act.
