Mr. Speaker, there are some features about this debate that are reminiscent of old-time revival meetings. I do not think there has ever been a question before the house on which there have been so many affirmative opinions given. It reminds me of a revival meeting in that one speaker after

Soldier Settlement
another rises to give testimony. So far as the effectiveness of the resolution is concerned I do not think it makes any difference whether it is or is not talked out, particularly after the display that has been given this afternoon and this evening.
I should like to join with others who have spoken in supporting this resolution, although as I read it there may be some detail in it, some point or another, with which I might disagree. When it comes to the resolution itself, however, I submit that it is in no way objectionable either under the rules and customs of this house or under the method adopted by the government in dealing with these matters. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is not in his place at the moment; probably he is engaged in the very serious business of preparing the budget. But even if he were here I hardly think he could say there was in this proposal anything in the nature of an attempt to raid the treasury.
I would point out that the resolution does not ' ask that certain moneys be spent; it uses the much more diplomatic method of recommending to the government that they take into consideration the advisability of, in effect, giving clear title to this land, and for that reason I think the government might very well look upon the resolution in a kindly way.
There is no doubt in the mind of any person, I believe, that returned men after the last war were mulcted of untold sums of money by the operation of the Soldier Settlement Act of that time. I have worked with men who for many years were on farms obtained under that scheme, men who struggled until they could struggle no longer in an endeavour to make the payments, and who finally had to give up. I distinctly remember one man who had been on the land for ten or twelve years, paying money year after year on a contract which never, under any circumstances, could he hope to complete. That, of course, was only one case; I know of many others. In the interval between that time and the present many may have obtained title to their land, but many others have given up and lost out after having put a great deal into it. We now have this small number remaining who are in the position described by the mover of this resolution, and it would seem to me to be a matter the government should take into very serious consideration, as to whether they should not give some final relief to these people who have laboured under this disability for so long.
I have not spoken for very long, so that I cannot be accused of endeavouring to talk out this proposition. On the contrary I have 47696-42
probably taken less time than many who have spoken from the opposite side of the house. I do not know that there is anything more that can be usefully said by me at the moment. I suggested in the beginning that this was a matter of simply giving testimony, and I wish to place myself on record as being in favour of doing everything possible that can be done under the circumstances of this case.
Mr. F. W. TOWNLEY-SMITH (North Battleford): Mr. Speaker, I should like to express myself as being wholeheartedly in favour of this resolution. I suppose nearly everything that can be said about it has been said, but I wish to add just a few words. I happen to have lived among some of these men who took farms after coming back from the first great war; as a matter of fact, four of them were on quarter-sections immediately adjoining my own farm. I watched their efforts; I saw their struggles and understood their difficulties, because they were also mine. They faced the hazards of farming: weather, frost and hail, drought, insect pests, plant diseases; all these encompassed these unfortunate people in exactly the same way as they did the rest of us, but they were quite unable to stand up under the strain. I watched their efforts, their progressive difficulties and their progressive failures. I saw their wives die under the strain. I saw their children attending school ill clad and poorly fed. I watched one generation fail to secure a fair education because of the poverty and difficulties under which their parents were labouring. All this I saw from my own doorstep. These people never had a chance. It is quite true that the fault did not lie entirely with the government. The hazards I have mentioned can never be blamed on any government, but they were there just the same. Probably one reason for the failure of these men lay in the fact that in some districts a quarter-section of land is not an economic farm; the overhead is too high for that acreage.
As I said, four of these men settled around my farm; none of them is there now. They have all gone and others are on those quarter-sections. That was twenty-six years ago, and it does seem to me that if, after struggling with the problem for twenty-six years, these men have been unable to straighten it out, the very least we could do would be to straighten it out for them and give them this land. They are no longer young. When they came there they were ambitious and cheerful; many of them were strong. Now their ages are from fifty to sixty years; and if in the last twenty-six years they have not been able

Soldier Settlement

to make a go of it, they will never be able to get straightened out now. Some hon. members have spoken about agriculture being in pretty good shape just now. If they would read their newspapers they would see that western agriculture, particularly in Saskatchewan, is having its own difficulties this year. They would read about two and four bushel crops, and some districts where there are no crops at all. Some areas have been fortunate and are having good crops, but taking the province as a whole conditions are not good.
There is one particular instance I should like to mention. A quarter-section of land was sold to a veteran at the going rate of $25 an acre. After some twenty years the veteran was compelled to leave that land, broken and bankrupt. The same quarter-section was immediately sold to another man by the soldier settlement board for $10 an acre. At $10 in the first place the veteran could have paid for it; at $25 he was unable to do so.
Some hon. members have been distressed over the wording of the preamble. May I suggest to them that they are not voting on the preamble but on the resolution, which reads:
That, in the opinion of .this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of giving clear titles to all soldier settlers who on March 31, 1944. held land under contract with .the soldier settlement board.
Hon. members, let us do this thing. Let us give these men one real good break.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise for the purpose of speaking on this motion, because I believe that what has been said so far did not touch the matter of principle which underlies the resolution. Without any doubt, our full sympathy goes to all those veterans who, after the first great war, took up land under the Veterans' Settlement Act. Those men, on their return from the war, certainly deserved whatever opportunities the government afforded them, but as I said a few moments ago, we are now dealing more particularly with a matter of principle and I think I am in a most favourable position to discuss it, since there are very few instances of such land settlement in the constituency I have the honour of representing.
The matter of principle Which underlies the present discussion seems to be the following: in taking up land the veteran entered with

the government into a contract which was perfectly free and quite voluntary. That contract was not forced upon him, it was signed under no pressure; everything was done on a purely voluntary basis. On the one hand, the government offered the veterans definite and distinct advantages, and on the other hand the veterans assumed some obligations, and agreed to terms and conditions clearly laid down in their contracts. Therefore, there is at stake a principle, which is linked up with the sanctity of contracts.
I do not believe we could interfere and ask that contracts that have been entered into in all freedom, and freely accepted by both parties be set aside merely on a resolution asking the government to take into consideration the advisability of giving clear titles to all soldier settlers for their land.
Mr. Speaker, this resolution appears to me as being prompted more by political considerations than by common sense. Indeed, it is only necessary to examine its wording to notice that it represents the present situation as being due to the "lack of adequate policy for agriculture". Of course I am not in a position to go over the whole farming policy of this government or of the liberal administrations which have preceded it, and I do not think this is the proper time to do so, but the least that can be said about the resolution is that it is an evidence of defeatism on the part of the hon. member who has moved it.
The motion before the house, rests on a question of simple justice: either the veteran has met his obligations, in which instance there are no complaints because every one is satisfied; or, he has failed to meet them for various reasons, such as bad weather, unfavourable international marketing conditions, competition and so on, but not necessarily from lack of an effective agricultural policy on the part of this country's government.
In that case, if the government grant a clear title to the veteran whose payments are in arrear, it will appear to me as a clear case of injustice to those who, under similar circumstances, have met their obligations. Then we might be confronted with the somewhat queer procedure of another motion asking the reimbursement of sums paid in by those who have not defaulted. No argument could prevent the moving of a resolution to that effect on the very same grounds. The parties concerned would have the same arguments of sympathy and sentiment; they could base their claims on their status as veterans and the hard times they have experienced. And then, for the second time, we would have to

Soldier Settlement
sanction an injustice flowing from the adoption of the motion before the house at this moment.
One thing is certain, the veterans of the first great war and those of the war just ended, do not ask for pity; all they want is fair treatment, nothing more.
Let us suppose for a moment that the present motion be carried. All the borrowers under the federal farm loan scheme, for example, who have defaulted in their payments, could come before the house, and, through another motion, request that their debts be cancelled, for reasons of sympathy, on account of hard times and especially because of the conditions engendered by the failure of the government to implement an efficient farm policy.
In the event the present motion is carried, we shall have established a precedent. Thus, there would be no valid reason to reject a similar resolution. From there on, whatever anyone would be in debt with the government, he could simply have to play on the sympathy and sentiments of the members of the house who would then be bound to grant his request.
Mr. Speaker, I believe sentimentality should be excluded from our discussions; we should take into account not the interest of a particular class of our citizens, but only the general welfare of the whole population. Everyone who would find it impossible to meet his obligations and would be faced with bankruptcy would have the right to apply to parliament for exceptional treatment and thus the House of Commons would become a dispenser of compassionate grants.
I respectfully suggest that the passage of such a resolution would inevitably lead us to state paternalism. Further, it would tend to give the veterans of this war, who are entitled to the advantages provided by the new settlement act, the wrong and false impression that if they fail to meet their obligations all they will have to do will be to come before Parliament in ten or fifteen years hence and request a remission or reduction of their debts. From a business standpoint, it would be creating a bad precedent; and I do not think that we should be moved by sentiment and become soft-hearted. Let us glance into the past and we shall find that the pioneers who came from France and who settled on the old lands of Quebec, on the island of Orleans and in the district of Riviere Ouelle and who, with their bare hands have built a whole country, did not receive any land clearing bonuses, or Government grants or remission of their debts 47696-m
from a paternalistic state; however, they built a whole country with the sweat of their brow, their labour and their devotion to duty.
Mr. Speaker, I feel we should recall the past and consider those facts. Accordingly, on a matter of principle, and disregarding any appeal to sentimentality, I place myself on record as being opposed to this resolution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not agree with the wording of the preamble to this resolution for reasons-that I do not think it necessary to state this-evening, but with the resolution itself I am in wholehearted agreement. It asks the government to take into consideration the advisability of giving clear titles to all soldier settlers who on March 31, 1944, held land under contract with the soldier settlement board.
Surely no hon. member can object to the government doing that. Surely no hon. member can object to the government reconsidering the whole matter and reviewing the whole subject. Not only do I think the government should reconsider and review the whole matter, but after they do that I hope they will see their way clear to give clear titles to these veterans as the resolution suggests.
I believe that a man should live up to his agreement and meet his obligations, but there are cases when it is quite impossible to do
Soldier Settlement

this. I am convinced that the situation in which these veterans find themselves is one of these cases.
I met a delegation of veterans that came to Ottawa in June of last year to present a brief asking that these men be given clear titles. I was more impressed by the men composing that delegation than by their brief. One had only to meet them and talk to them to be impressed by the justice of their claim. One had only to look at them to realize that for years past they had faced a tremendously difficult task, that they had struggled with courage against great odds and had done the best they could under the most adverse circumstances. It was clear that the cards had been stacked against them and that fate had been unkind.
After talking to these men I realized that we could not afford to allow them to leave the land as they were doing. I realized we would be making a great mistake if we let men of their character and their racial origin and their families leave the land and perhaps have it taken over by other persons who might not and probably would not be so willing to come to the defence of their king and country in time of war.
I think the agreements that were entered into could well be changed in favour of the veterans on- the ground of mutual mistake. The mistake on the part of the board was that they overvalued the farms in the first instance and sold them to veterans at too high a price. The mistake on the pant of the veterans was that they thought the farms would produce a great deal more revenue than they did. The mistake was owing to the fact that the farms had been purchased by the board and sold to the veterans in boom times and in a period of inflation.
This matter does not affect veterans who live in the prairie provinces only, because, as the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) pointed out this afternoon, there are veterans in the maritime provinces who have faced similar difficulties. I could cite instances, although I do not propose to do so this evening. I would urge the government not only to reconsider and review the whole matter but to give these veterans clear title to their lands.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in the discussion on the resolution now before the house as a soldier and not as a veteran, although the title of veteran has been attributed to me by the press ever since I have become a member of the House of Commons. I feel, however, that a veteran is one who has returned from

a theatre of war or has experienced action on the battlefield. Although I enlisted as a volunteer, I have never had the privilege, through no fault of my own, to go across the sea and fight with my comrades against the enemy which was trying to deny not only to Canada but to the entire world that peace and freedom which have always been dear to those who live under democratic government. Neverthelss, as a soldier, I feel that I should express my opinion on the resolution now before us.
The resolution asks the government to wipe out a legal debt owing to this country, and as such, it presents a very serious problem which should be given careful consideration, by all hon. members, no matter on which side of the house they sit.
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) upon his sincerity and tenacity in bringing this resolution before the house. I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) ask that immediate consideration be given to the request as submitted by the hon. member for Battle River. As he did establish himself under the Soldier Settlement Act which was passed by the government in power after the great war of 1914-18, and being thrifty, hardworking and an honest and conscientious farmer was able to pay back his debt to the government, that does not mean necessarily that all the debts still owed to the government for the same privileges that he himself enjoyed after the war of 1914-18 should be wiped off.
I also wish to congratulate the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr,. Diefenbaker), whose political career in the House of Commons I have followed closely when an outsider, and for whom I have always had a great admiration for the attitude he has taken in this house in discussing this problem which concern the welfare of Canada's veterans.
It must be remembered that when the government in power after the last war introduced the Soldier Settlement Act, they did so without any experience whatsoever in that field. That was really the first time that Canada, had sent troops overseas to join with our allies in defeating the Germans. The government when they passed that act yvere very sincere and thought they had passed an act from which every veteran of the war of 1914-18 who came under it would benefit, and that no request would be made to have the act amended as has been frequently done from 1922 up until this day.

Soldier Settlement
It must also be remembered that during the period 1918-19 the wheat acreage in this country-I am speaking of western Canada- expanded, but in the southern area of the western provinces there was a large drought area where the board did not allow settlement by veterans who applied to get the full privileges granted by the Soldier Settlement Act. After the war of 1914-18 we had inflation for about a year and a half in Canada, and then the drought areas in western Canada came back. After the great war we still had a very large wheat surplus, but on account of the war ending so abruptly in 1918 there existed no purchasing power in Europe and we were unable to dispose of our agricultural products. That condition was accentuated by the fact that practically all existing governments, thinking they were placing their own economy on a sound basis, increased tariffs as high as Canada did under the regime of the Bennett government from 1930 to 1935. Therefore we were not able to sell our products to the other countries of the world.
In 1922, after many requests for amendments had been received from veterans of the war of 1914-18 who had settled under the Soldier Settlement Act, the government brought in an amendment which resulted in the interest on the debt owed by the veterans being waived for periods of from two to four years, depending upon the settler's date of establishment. Then in 1925 another amendment was made to the Soldier Settlement Act granting a reduction to the soldier settlers of forty per cent of the cost of the live stock purchased prior to October 1, 1920, and a reduction of twenty per cent of the cost of live stock purchased after October 1, 1920, and prior to October 1, 1921.
At a still later date, in 1927-in the meantime there had been a rise in the cost of living and in the cost of all commodities needed by every Canadian-a further amendment was made granting a reduction of the amount by which the price of the purchased farm exceeded 1927 values. That also was of great benefit to the soldier settlers. That was followed in 1930 by a reduction of thirty per cent of all the debts owed to the soldier settlement board.
Hon. members will notice that even though the Conservative government which was then in power was followed by the Liberals, and the Conservative government came back in 1930, an unbiased attitude was taken by all governments in power concerning the debts owed the country by the veterans who settled
under the act. From 1930 to 1935 when the Conservative party was in power a remission was granted of one year's interest on all charges and also a dollar for dollar bonus respecting payment of all obligations then owing to the board; that is, for all debts falling due before April 1, 1936, which date was later extended, on further representations, to March 31, 1941.
During the Bennett regime was introduced the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act which granted benefits not only to farmers but also to veterans who had settled under the Soldier Settlement Act, which legislation was brought into force by the Conservative party. I worked under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and I know of the benefits received by the farmers of western Canada under that act. While I do not want to mention any case, I know of applications filed in the office, where I was assistant official receiver under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, of the benefits gained, when the case was brought before the board of review. The grants given to the veterans were really of great advantage to them. They consolidated the debt owing at the time at which the application was discussed before the board of review, and extensions for payment were granted up to ten, fifteen and twenty years at very low interest rates. But in 1942 there were still a great number of cases that remained unpaid through no fault of the veteran. Some soldiers had already reenlisted in the armed forces of the great war of 19391945, and there were others who, owing to sickness and also by reason of wounds received in the war of 1914-1918, or family troubles, or from other social causes, still had to apply to the government to receive certain relief in respect of debts owing under the act. That is why in 1942 the government authorized the treasury board, on the recommendation of the director, to reduce the indebtedness of the settler to the present and prospective value of the land. They were given time to file application until December 31, 1943, and even then, as I have stated, a great number of these settlers had reenlisted in this conflict and as such were unable to file application. But they were still granted the same rights, and recently I was informed that the government had given power to grant an extension; where no applications had been made, owing to no fault of the men; owing to service in this war or sickness, they were given the same privilege as granted those who applied in 1942.
I feel that the amount involved is not very high, but the fact remains that it is still a debt owing just like a debt owing to-day by
Soldier Settlement

a farmer who might apply for a mortgage to any company who might advance money to farmers to purchase land, stock, machinery or cattle. I feel that the resolution as worded should never have been brought before the house but that the government must give the matter consideration; and as I have stated, certain action has already been taken in that respect in granting extension to farmers to pay their debts owing to the country in respect of the benefit they received on settling on lands in Canada for their services in the war of 1914-1918. As such the veterans coming back from this war will then feel able to file application and receive the same benefits granted under the Veterans' Land Act which was passed in 1942 as granted to the veterans settled under the Soldier Settlement Act in connection with the war of 1914-1918.

I wish to express one or two sentiments on the resolution introduced so ably by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair). I believe it was the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) who said he represented an island in the Pacific. Well, I come from an island in the east, Prince Edward Island, and I think it might interest the house for me to tell of some 'of the experiences of veterans who took up land under the Soldier Settlement Act after the last war. I well recall many instances where these men were put on lands valued at three or four times their price. It was impossible for them to make good and they naturally failed.
I do not wish hon. members to misunderstand me. I agree heartily with most of the sentiments expressed this afternoon and evening, but I think the resolution as at present worded is most inadequate. In the first place, a measure of relief such as this should be uniform in its benefits, and the thing that strikes me about this resolution is the great disparity of benefits that will accrue from it. There will be no case where the equity in the land will be the same and therefore each individual will derive a different benefit under the resolution.
In the second place, some of the previous speakers have referred to the annoyances that may be expressed by those veterans who have already got title. Well, what about the poor lad who held on for quite a long while and then gave up? For that reason I submit that the resolution is totally inadequate because the benefits are not equal and fair.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs

speechtext:
One of the impressions that have been created by some speakers who have taken part in the debate this afternoon and to-night is that previous parliaments have consisted of men who had no interest in the returned soldier and were quite callous to what was happening to him. In fact, one hon. member has given expression to this thought: "I am interested in people and that is why I am here in this house." I have the honour and privilege of speaking now in the third parliament in which I have been a member, and I think I can say to that hon. member that in those other parliaments there were members elected to speak here who were also interested in people and interested in trying to do what was right by the people they represented and particularly by those who fought for our country in the first world war.
I am very glad that an attempt has been made to indicate something of what has been done for the returned soldier since world war I. It has been a popular pastime of some people to pretend that nothing whatever was done for the returned soldier. It has been said so often that I am sure some people have been led to believe that, no matter how carefully parliament has endeavoured to provide for the rehabilitation and reestablishment of the returned soldier of this war, they will also find that they have not been properly looked after. That is a natural assumption to make from the talk that has gone on among so many people in the last ten or fifteen years. However, I do not think the boys who went overseas in the last war are convinced that all the parliaments between the two wars were callous about their condition and did not do the best they could, and that suddenly a new race of men, with one woman added, has come into being here and will make all the difference in this parliament. If the idea is created that parliament is helpless and unwilling to do justice to those who have fought for the country, then a service is not done to parliament in any way, shape or form, and confidence is not created in the ability of this parliament and the willingness of parliament and the government representing it to do justly by those whom we are going to reestablish during the next four or five years.
As has been pointed out in this debate, there is no doubt that the people who set up the Soldier Settlement Act after the last war thought they were setting up an act that would work. They ran into the conditions

Soldier Settlement
which are described in the resolution and with which most of us will agree. The preamble to the resolution reads:
. . . have in many instances suffered severe hardships because of purchase of land, live stock and equipment at inflationary prices, and low prices received for farm products. . . .
With that statement I think most hon. members will agree, and as a result the various changes were made which have been enumerated by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Viau). That is the first point which I would wish to make. All those parliaments were honestly endeavouring to deal with the situation as they found it. One of the things that moved those parliaments was that as between the returned soldiers who took up land under this act there should be an attempt to make adjustments which would benefit as much as possible all, that no adjustment would be justified if it discriminated between one group and another. I am satisfied that the only way we can justify in the eyes of the country any expenditure which we make is if it appears to deal justly with the people who have been endeavouring to pay for their land during the last four or five years. That is one of the things which I am sure will strike home to hon. members, namely, the fact that the man who during the last four or five years has struggled hard to pay for his land and has got clear title will say, if his neighbour next door, who perhaps has thought that ultimately the debt would be cancelled and has paid little or nothing, gets clear title, that he has not been dealt with justly. We then will have that claim made.
Be that as it may, I should like to lay before hon. members the effect of the various improvements which have been made in the situation from time to time and which have been enumerated by the hon. member for St. Boniface. Starting with the year 1922 and going on to the year 1944, these improvements have amounted roughly to $45 million, which were written off the debt of the soldier settlers of this country. The original indebtedness for the capital advanced was roughly $109 million. Therefore almost the equivalent of fifty per cent of the original capital advanced has been written off. I give this figure to do justice to previous parliaments; they were not callous about these things, and they did work for the returned soldier to the best of their ability.
With regard to the present situation, I would draw to the attention of the hon. members the fact that we have on the order paper a resolution which provides:
That a select committee be appointed,
1. To consider all legislation passed since the commencement of the war with the German reich relating to the pensions, treatment, and reestablishment of former members of His Majesty's armed forces and of other persons who have otherwise engaged in pursuits closely related to war.
I take it that this will provide for the setting up of a committee on returned soldiers' affairs, which will be very much like the committees which have sat in the last two parliaments and on which I have -had the great honour and privilege of serving. These committees were made up largely of returned soldiers. They were noted not only by the members of all parties on the committees themselves, but by those who watched their operations, as committees which were perhaps the most non-partisan of any which sat on any problem during that period of nine years. I would say this to the new members who come into this house and who are inclined to lecture those who sat here in previous parliaments, that we sat many, many hours and gave very anxious consideration to the representations which were made by the authorized representatives of the returned soldiers throughout the country. Many changes were recommended to the committee, changes which were consistent with the recommendations of those recognized returned soldiers' organizations. These changes were recommended by the committees and accepted by the government. The government has now provided for the setting up of another committee. I believe there are now eighty-four men in the house who have given services to the country in the armed service in the first world war and in this war. Unless we have a committee that is much larger than usual we shall not be able to put all the ex-servicemen on that committee. I am very proud that the government is ready to trust the legislation in regard to ex-service men in large measure to the hands of at least one-third of the membership of this house who have actually served their country in the armed forces.
I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that that committee will have a chance to study this whole question; it will have a chance to hear the representatives of the various returned soldiers' organizations in the country, and what they have to say about it. It will have a chance to go into the way the acts have been administered; it will have a chance to examine into whether the officials of the soldier settlement board have discharged their duties with a
Soldier Settlement

reasonable amount of consideration for the humanities of the situation. There will be on that committee returned soldiers from all parties and, if it is anything like previous committees, there will be the freest discussion on all those problems. Therefore I would say to the hon. member who moved this resolution that to have it properly considered I think it will be admitted that the place where that can be done will be before that committee where .we can get the actual facts, get witnesses in front of the committee and hear what actually has been done.
I would ask the house to consider all the legislation that has been passed in regard to those who served with His Majesty's forces. In that legislation there is order in council P.C. 10472. In that order in council it was provided that any returned soldier could apply to the director of the soldier settlement board for a reduction of his debt. Then the appraisers of the board made a careful examination of the situation. They valued the land and made a report not only on the land but on the chance of the returned soldier paying the debt within a reasonable time; on his health, and on his record during the previous number of years. On the basis of this report the director was able to recommend a reduction which would give that returned soldier a chance to clear himself of debt within a reasonable time, based not only upon the value of the land but upon personal considerations as well. Then the treasury board was given power, on the basis of the recommendation, to write down the debt accordingly.
I understand that that order in council has been given a very liberal application, but the facts in that connection can be ascertained when this committee meets. If it is proved that the policy of the government in this matter has not been carried out liberally it will be the business of this committee to find out the facts and recommend accordingly. In any event, under that order in council an amount of 1988,205.54 was written off the debts of the soldier settlers. Under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act a total of $6,808,536 was written off. As I understand the law, any soldier settlement farmer in the prairie provinces who has not applied for and obtained an adjustment of his debts can apply under that act for an adjustment; and anyone who has observed the workings of the boards set up in western Canada under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act will know that they have been very considerate and very liberal in their write-downs of debt.
So that the soldier had the chance to apply to the director of the soldier settlement

board or under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act for a write-down of his debt. He also has the right to make a second application under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act if he obtained an adjustment before December 31, 1938. Some people did not apply under either provisions. As I understand the law, they can still apply under the Farmers' Creditors Act, and have the matter of adjusting their debts brought under the machinery of that legislation. I have had a certain amount of experience of the basis on which the officials acting under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act write down debts in regard to soldier settlers. It is not done entirely on the basis of the value of the land. They take into consideration the record of the settler, his proved ability to discharge his obligations and so on, and they have written the debt down to a level where he could hope to be entirely free of debt within a reasonably short time.
Those provisions have been made, but in order to give another chance to those who have not made any application at all to have their debt written down, this government passed an order in council on the 28th of last month. I need not read the entire order in council, but it provided that those who had not applied through no fault of their own could still apply to the director of the soldier settlement board to have consideration given to the writing down of their debt, and gave the treasury board power to write it down.

Yes, three days ago. The effective part of the order in council reads:

That is P.C. 10472.
[DOT]-be amended to March 31, 194G; and that, decision as to whether the failure of any settler to make application on or before December 31, 1943-
That was the former cut-off date.
-was or was not due to reasons beyond the control of any such settler shall be at the discretion of the director of soldier settlement.
With the consent of the house, and in the name of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), since I have not read the whole of the order in council I should like to table it.
Bearing in mind all that has been said and what I have just mentioned to the house as to what has been done and what has been provided for, I suggest that a proper approach to this problem would be to say, we will

Soldier Settlement
have a committee made up, I expect, almost entirely of ex-servicemen, who will have a chance to go into the administration of these various orders in council and the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. They will be able to look into these cases which are alleged not to have been properly dealt with under the existing machinery. Anyone who has had experience with the trial of cases knows that no judge will act in a serious matter on ex parte evidence, without hearing all sides That is a fundamental principle of British justice, that all sides of a case shall be heard. When I hear hon. members say, "We do not know what has been done; we do not know the actual facts, but we know someone claims to have been mistreated and therefore we are going to make a sweeping decision", then I suggest that at any rate it would do no harm to wait until a committee of this house composed of returned soldiers has had a chance to hear whether or not the returned soldier organizations of this country are in favour of this proposal. It can do no harm, to give that committee a chance to look into these cases and see whether the paid servants of the government are not properly carrying out their duties, whether they are actually abusing those who defended this country in the first great war.
These are matters in which I believe we, as members of parliament, should be interested. We should ask to hear both sides before we undertake to act. It has been suggested that this soldier settlement scheme has been an entire and utter failure. Well, I am free to admit that owing to lack of former experience and owing to a desire to put the act into operation too quickly, mistakes were made. It was attempted to settle some 19.000 of these soldiers on the land in a matter of about eighteen months. Now, of course, we have learned by the mistakes made after the last war. From what I have seen of the boys coming back from overseas, they are not going to rush into things quite as quickly as was the case with those coming back after the first great war. I have talked to several returned men recently, and their attitude is that land values may be a little higher now than they will be two or three years from now, that perhaps equipment costs a little more now than it will cost in another year or two. As I understand it, this act will be so administered as to encourage the boys coming back from overseas to take their time before plunging into this proposition; to look around for a piece of land where they feel sure they can make a success, and not go into it until the time comes when they can get their land and equipment at
reasonable prices. There will be no attempt to try to get all these gentlemen settled within a period of a year and a half. In other words, there will be an attempt to put everybody into a position where, if he is settled under the Veterans' Land Act, he will have a real chance of success-almost a 100 per cent chance of success.
There is a tendency to suggest that the various measures which this government -has put into force, and which, I would draw to the attention of those people who jeer at those measures, have been approved by the people of Canada in the last general election, are not sufficient. I see the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum) laughing at that. I will ask her this question: Did she get half the people of Canada to endorse her attitude toward this legislation?

I am referring to the
Veterans' Land Act which was passed in 1942. I have already indicated some of the reasons why I am satisfied that that act will be a success. First, there is to be a careful examination into the qualifications of those who apply under the act. An effort will be made to see that they are fully qualified to make a success at farming. If not, courses in farming will be available in order that they may become qualified before they actually go on the land and risk their money.

Soldier Settlement
Then, no attempt will be made to place them on the land within the first twelve months after the war has ended. Time will be taken to make sure that land is obtained at fair prices and that people have a chance to select the land they want. The men will be given help to get settled on good land and an effort will be made to see that exorbitant prices are not paid for such land and for machinery and other items. It was in this connection that veterans of the last war found themselves at a great disadvantage. They paid high prices for land and machinery, and after a period of four or five years they found that the land and machinery was worth only a fraction of what had been paid for them. That was enough to discourage any one.
Another aspect of the matter is the protection given to the veteran in connection with what he will get for what he produces. A floor has been placed under farm prices. As the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture said, this is the most radical reform measure that has ever been passed by any parliament in Canada. I have great faith in the effectiveness of the floor under farm prices bill, and I have great faith that it will provide real protection to the veterans in the years that lie ahead.
Then we have the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which will protect the veteran farmer on the prairies in the event of crop failure. I often think of the years from 1930 to 1939 when we had crop failure after crop failure in Saskatchewan and what it would have meant had we had the Prairie Farm Assistance Act at that time. Is it any wonder that thoughtful people think of the things that have been done by the present government? Is it any wonder that a good share of them stood by the Liberal party in the last election even though our election system resulted in only two Liberals being elected? However, I would remind my Tory friends that they managed to elect only one, so that there is nothing there about which they can crow. Incidently I will tell them that one of the reasons why that man was elected was, first, that he is an outstanding man and, second, that he assured his electors that he was just as liberal as any Liberal running in Saskatchewan.
There are other grounds, but I have not the time to go into them to-night. I regret that I have not the time. I have not mentioned the Family Allowances Act.
